The clinical presentation is highly characteristic of syringomyelia: chronic, progressive, bilateral upper limb burning pain and paresthesias (reflecting involvement of the spinothalamic tracts at the level of the syrinx), coupled with distal motor weakness (hand intrinsics) due to anterior horn cell damage within the expanding syrinx cavity. The MRI-confirmed cervicothoracic syrinx is the central structural abnormality. While syrinx can arise from multiple causes (e.g., post-traumatic, neoplastic, inflammatory, idiopathic), the *most common* and *most likely* etiology in an adult with a cervicothoracic syrinx — especially without clear trauma, tumor, or inflammatory markers — is Chiari I malformation. Critically, the absence of classic Chiari symptoms (e.g., occipital headache, lower cranial nerve signs) does *not* rule it out: up to 30–50% of adults with Chiari I and syrinx are asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic for the hindbrain anomaly itself; the syrinx-related myelopathic symptoms often dominate the clinical picture.
